prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- A woman steps outside and disintegrates into loose particles that scatter in the eastern breeze.
- Fragments of her body spread across the highway, her neighbor, her car, and her garden, causing strange and vivid effects.
- As days pass without rain, the dispersed woman reflects that despite encompassing so much, she accomplishes very little.
- She tries unsuccessfully to understand why she disintegrated, while memories of earlier hours evade her like colorful lizards.
- Her scattered remains eventually rise and converge in the sky, where an observer mistakes her for an interesting cloud.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A woman inexplicably disintegrates into windblown particles and tries to understand her condition while observing her remains disperse through the world. Ultimately, her dust gathers into a cloud, suggesting that dissolution transforms individual identity into something vast, strange, and casually misperceived by others.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Days, Each, Strange

outputs.L1:
A woman stepped outside, crumbled into loose particulate, and, as the breeze blew in from the east, scattered: her handful of heart, volcanic ash, spiraled along the highway, and five of her teeth slipped between her neighbor’s breasts. Her neighbor unbuttoned her blouse to scratch at her suddenly red, luminous skin.

Days passed. Each day, the sun drifted distractedly from chair to chair; each night, the stars—old scatterbrains—commiserated. It did not rain.

Strange, the granular woman thought to herself. Although I encompass so much, I accomplish so little.

Her car sparkled with her hair and bones; her garden thrived. She tried to think: Why did this happen? What had I eaten? Why was I bothered? Those old hours—spotted and exotic lizards—darted across the gravel, flicking through their skin colors as one flicks through channels on a TV. She could not catch a single one.

Then, like a flock of sparrows converging upon the skull of an oak, all her twittering dust—her brain, bone, and the dangerous shreds of her fingers—clawed toward the sky.

“What an interesting cloud,” someone said.
outputs.L2:
A woman walked outdoors and collapsed into drifting grains. When an easterly wind rose, it carried her away: the small measure of her heart, like cinders from a volcano, whirled along the highway, while five teeth lodged in the cleavage of the woman next door. The neighbor opened her blouse so she could rub the skin, which had abruptly become crimson and radiant.

Several days went by. The sun wandered absentmindedly between chairs every morning, and each evening the stars—forgetful old souls—offered their sympathy. No rain fell.

How peculiar, the woman of particles reflected. I extend across such a vast space, yet manage to do almost nothing. Her hair and skeleton glittered across her automobile, and her garden flourished. She attempted to understand: What caused this? What food had she consumed? Why had it upset her?

Those former hours resembled unusual, speckled lizards racing over the gravel, changing the colors of their hides as quickly as someone flips through television channels. She was unable to capture any of them.

At last, like sparrows gathering in the crown of an oak, every murmuring fragment of her—her mind, her bones, and the perilous splinters of her fingers—scrabbled upward into the heavens.

“What a fascinating cloud,” someone remarked.
outputs.L3:
A woman steps outside one morning and, without warning, disintegrates. Her body loosens into countless fine particles, which are caught at once by the eastern breeze and carried away.

The fragments spread across the neighborhood in every direction. Some settle on the highway, glittering among the lanes and causing passing drivers to glimpse impossible colors in their mirrors. Some land on her neighbor, who suddenly feels an inexplicable rush of forgotten tenderness. Others coat her car, making its metal surface shimmer as though it contains a private sunset. Still more drift into her garden, where the flowers grow vivid and strange, opening into shapes no botanist has ever named.

Days pass, and no rain falls to gather or wash her away. Dispersed across roads, objects, people, and plants, the woman remains conscious of everything she touches. Yet she begins to feel dissatisfied. Although she now encompasses more of the world than she ever did while confined to a single body, she accomplishes almost nothing. She can observe, influence, and faintly transform, but she cannot act with purpose.

Again and again, she tries to understand why she disintegrated. She searches backward through her memory for some warning or cause, but the hours before she stepped outside refuse to stay still. They dart beyond her reach like brightly colored lizards, flashing blue, green, and gold before vanishing into cracks.

At last, her scattered remains begin to stir. The particles lift from the highway, her neighbor’s clothes, the car, and the garden. Rising on currents of warm air, they converge high above the earth, gathering into a single luminous mass. Far below, an observer looks up, pauses, and points toward the sky.

“What an interesting cloud,” the observer says, as the woman drifts silently overhead.
outputs.L4:
Mara began to come apart on a Tuesday morning.

There was no pain. That was the first strange thing.

She had just stepped outside with a cup of coffee when the wind moved through her. Not around her coat or beneath her hair, but through the center of her body, as if she were an open door. Her fingers loosened around the cup. Before it struck the pavement, the skin of her hand lifted in a pale spray.

She watched it go.

Tiny particles spun above the railing, bright in the morning sun. More followed: the fine bones of her fingers, the blue threads of her veins, the bitten half-moons of her nails. All of it became dry, weightless matter. The coffee cup shattered at her feet, but she heard the sound from a curious distance.

Mara tried to cry out. Her mouth scattered before it could shape a word.

Within seconds, the woman standing on the steps was gone. In her place hovered a wavering outline of dust. For an instant she retained her shape: shoulders, head, arms raised in alarm. Then a gust swept along the street, and the outline collapsed.

Part of her settled in the flower bed. Part clung to the wet shards of the cup. Most of her rose over the railing and was carried away.

She remained conscious.

That was the second strange thing.

Mara felt herself divided without feeling diminished. She was in the grit beneath the hedge and in the powder turning above the rooftops. She was caught in a spiderweb under the eaves. She was sailing down the street in a loose brown veil.

She could not decide where to look because she was looking from everywhere.

A bus passed, drawing some of her into its wake. She streamed behind it through three intersections. A cyclist rode through her, coughing once into his sleeve. A child waiting at a crossing lifted her face and laughed as the dust swirled around her.

“Look,” the child said. “A tiny tornado.”

Mara wanted to tell her that she was not a tornado. She was thirty-nine years old. She worked in municipal accounting. She disliked olives and loved thunderstorms. She had a scar beneath her left knee from falling on a bottle when she was twelve. Her mother called every Sunday at seven. Her apartment contained six dying plants and a drawer full of batteries she could never remember buying.

She repeated these facts to herself, afraid that without a body to store them they would blow away too.

I am Mara Vale, she thought.

But the thought came from a thousand moving grains, and her name sounded less certain each time.

By noon, she had spread across half the city.

Some of her entered an office tower through an open window and settled over a conference table. A man drew a line through her with one finger while discussing quarterly losses. Some fell into a bakery, where a woman wiped her from the glass case with a damp cloth. Some drifted onto the river and darkened, particle by particle, before sinking beneath the surface.

Underwater, Mara found herself among weeds, coins, fish bones, and the silt of older things. She wondered whether those things were conscious too. Perhaps the whole world had been thinking silently all along: stone, rust, ash, the powder beneath furniture.

Perhaps bodies only made people arrogant.

Her largest portion remained near home. Neighbors gathered around the broken cup and the empty coat that had collapsed on the steps. Someone called the police. Someone else called her mother.

Mara watched an officer shake out the coat. A soft cloud rose from its lining—more of her—and the officer sneezed.

There was an investigation. There were questions about enemies, medications, gas leaks, cults, and experimental chemicals. A reporter stood on the pavement that evening and described Mara’s disappearance as “baffling.” Behind him, a cleaning crew washed the last visible traces of her into the gutter.

Her mother arrived after dark.

She stood beneath the porch light with both hands pressed against her chest. She did not weep at first. She only looked at the steps, as though Mara might return if given enough time.

A little of Mara rested on the porch rail. She tried to gather herself. She tried to rise and form a hand, a face, anything her mother might recognize.

The effort produced only a faint spiral.

Her mother brushed at the air.

“There’s dust everywhere,” she murmured.

Then she began to cry.

The words hurt more than disintegration had.

For several days Mara resisted the wind. She lodged herself in corners. She adhered to grease, rainwater, wool, and skin. She tried to preserve boundaries: this grain is me, that grain is not. Yet the distinction became increasingly difficult.

In the gutter, she mixed with pollen and brick dust. On the riverbed, she mingled with clay. At a construction site, she joined plaster, concrete, and powdered stone. She entered the lungs of strangers and left them again in breath.

The city carried her beyond itself.

Trucks took her north in the treads of their tires. Birds bore her on their feathers. Rain lifted her from streets and delivered her to drains, streams, reservoirs, roots. A seed opened in soil that contained a trace of her. Months later, part of Mara became the green vein of a leaf.

Was that still her?

She did not know.

She began to forget the exact shape of her hands. Her apartment became a floor plan without warmth. Her own face survived only as a set of details: dark eyes, a narrow chin, one eyebrow slightly higher than the other. Even her name seemed small and artificial, a label attached to something that had never truly been separate.

Yet other memories sharpened.

She remembered every breeze she had ignored.

She remembered dust moving in a bar of sunlight while her father swept the kitchen. She remembered flour blooming above a mixing bowl, ash lifting from a campfire, snow crossing a road at night. She had thought of each as shapeless matter. She had never imagined that dispersal might have a point of view.

Years passed, though time no longer reached all of her equally.

One particle lay sealed beneath fresh paint and knew only darkness. Another crossed an ocean in the upper atmosphere. Another remained beneath her mother’s refrigerator until the apartment was emptied after her mother’s death.

That grain rose when the refrigerator was dragged aside.

For one instant, Mara remembered Sunday telephone calls with unbearable clarity.

Then the vacuum took her.

She learned not to mourn each separation. Nothing stayed anywhere. Mountains entered rivers. Rivers entered blood. Skin entered bedsheets, bedsheets entered fire, fire entered sky. The world was not made of objects, she understood, but of departures.

And arrivals.

High above the ocean, currents began to draw her scattered particles together.

Not all of them came. Much of Mara remained in roots, walls, lungs, mud, and sealed rooms. But enough converged to create a dimness in the air. Dust gathered around salt. Moisture gathered around dust. Droplets formed, each holding some minute remnant of the woman who had once stood outside with coffee in her hand.

The gathering had no single center. It did not resemble recovery. Mara was not rebuilding herself.

She was becoming weather.

She spread across the horizon, enormous and gray-white. Sunlight moved through her in radiant columns. Within her, cold air folded over warm. Electric charge trembled between regions of her vast new body.

Below, ships altered course.

On a beach, people pointed upward.

One man said the cloud looked like a hand. A woman beside him said it looked like a horse. A boy insisted it was a dragon, though no one else could see it.

Mara heard them all.

She might have been offended once. She might have wanted to explain that she was not a hand, a horse, or a dragon. She was Mara Vale. She was a daughter. She was a vanished woman. She was the answer to a mystery no one had solved.

But these statements no longer contradicted the others.

She was also river silt and leaf tissue. She was dust beneath paint. She was saltwater, smoke, mineral, rain. She was the shadow crossing the beach and the silver edge where sunlight touched vapor.

The people below watched for a few minutes. Then someone opened a cooler. Someone complained that the forecast had promised clear skies. Towels were folded. Children chased one another along the surf.

No one recognized her.

The cloud moved inland.

By evening, it had grown dark enough to trouble the birds. Wind bent the trees. Windows closed one by one. Far below, a woman collecting laundry felt the first drop strike her cheek.

“Rain,” she said, mildly surprised.

Then Mara fell across the earth.
outputs.L5:
**Strange Days**

Each morning, the town woke beneath a different sky. Some days it was violet, other days green, and once it shimmered like a silver mirror.

No one knew why—except Mara.

Each night, she climbed the hill beyond the houses and turned the rusted wheel hidden beneath the old oak tree. She never knew what the wheel would change. Only that if she stopped, morning might not come at all.

These were strange days, certainly.

But they were days nonetheless, and each one felt like a gift.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a woman who steps outside and disintegrates into dust, scattering across her neighborhood while remaining conscious.
counterfactuals.output:
When Mara stepped outside, the morning mistook her for an old wall.

First her hands loosened into powder. Then her shoulders sighed apart. Her face became a pale weather, her dress collapsing empty on the porch as the rest of her lifted—softly, without panic—into the neighborhood.

She remained awake in every grain.

Part of her settled on the baker’s window, where loaves rose like sleeping suns. Part entered the lungs of a boy bicycling to school, and for one bright block she rang with the silver bell of his breath. She gathered in gutters, learned the dark grammar of rainwater, clung to the black fur of a cat who carried her beneath a hedge full of blue bottles and lost buttons.

How strange, she thought, to have no center.

Her left eye dusted the mayor’s roses. Her childhood drifted into the laundromat and turned slowly with the sheets. Her name lodged beneath a widow’s fingernail. By noon, Mara was on every doorstep, tasting salt, shoe leather, pollen, rust. She heard a hundred kitchens opening their cupboards. She felt quarrels tremble through floorboards. She knew which houses held music and which held silence folded carefully in drawers.

The wind arrived after lunch and scattered her farther.

She crossed the playground in a golden veil. Children ran through her, shrieking, and she remembered having bones. She rose above chimneys, entered attics, touched the small abandoned kingdoms beneath beds. Everywhere, people swept at her.

Still, she loved them.

By evening, the neighborhood glittered with her absence. Each porch wore a little of her. Each leaf held one lucid particle. The moon came up and found her distributed among the ordinary things: fence posts, moth wings, soup steam, the wet noses of dogs.

Mara tried to say, I am here.

All along the street, curtains stirred.

And though no one understood, everyone paused—spoon lifted, book open, hand on a lamp switch—suddenly certain that the dust in the room was listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph piece of magical realism in which a woman becomes particulate matter, with vivid bodily imagery, personified celestial objects, and an ambiguous ending.
counterfactuals.output: At dawn, while kneading bread in the blue-tiled kitchen, Mara felt her fingertips loosen into flour-fine motes, each grain carrying a whorl of skin, a crescent of nail, the faint salt of her blood; she watched without fear as her wrists thinned into drifting pollen and her veins unspooled in red threads that floated toward the open window, where the moon, pale and sleepless, pressed its worried face against the glass. By noon her ribs had become a small white weather, rattling softly above the table, and her heart, divided into a thousand crimson specks, continued beating in the sunbeams, so that the whole room pulsed. Outside, the sun bent low like a gossiping neighbor and asked the rooftops what had happened, while Venus covered her mouth with both hands and the stars, though invisible, whispered her name into the chimneys. Mara’s husband returned at dusk to find her dress standing upright beside the oven, full of warm, shimmering dust; when he reached for it, the particles rose, smelling of yeast and rain, and streamed into his nostrils, his eyes, the pores of his outstretched palms. That night he dreamed—or remembered—that she was walking across the ceiling, whole and luminous, yet in the morning there were footprints in the flour, leading from the bed to the window, and no one could say whether they went out or came in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an unsettling, lyrical flash-fiction passage about bodily dissolution, memory, weather, and transformation. Use dreamlike metaphors and finish with a bystander mistaking the woman’s remains for a cloud.
counterfactuals.output:
By noon, the rain had learned her name.

It tapped the syllables along her spine until the bones loosened like old piano keys. She stood in the field remembering rooms that no longer existed: her mother’s blue cup, a window breathing winter, the small red shoe of a child she had never had. Each memory surfaced beneath her skin, pale and startled, then dissolved into weather.

Her hair lifted first, unthreading into black wind. Her fingers thinned to rivulets and ran through the grass, carrying fingerprints into the roots. When she opened her mouth, fog poured out—the taste of pennies, milk, and distant thunder—and with it went every word she had kept secret.

She did not fall. She became less certain.

Her ribs opened like wet shutters. Moths fluttered from the dark chamber of her chest, each bearing a face she had loved and forgotten. By evening, only a trembling whiteness remained above the field, snagged on the branches, luminous with the shape of her leaving.

A man on the road glanced up, buttoned his coat against the coming storm, and mistook what was left of the woman for a cloud.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine that a woman crumbles into ash and is carried by an east wind. Describe where her teeth, hair, bones, heart, and thoughts end up, using poetic, surreal language.
counterfactuals.output:
Her teeth fall first, white seeds scattered into the furrows of the western sea, where blind fish wear them as crowns.

Her hair unspools across the sky, threading itself through the needles of pine trees until every forest whispers in her voice.

Her bones become pale bridges beneath the earth, crossed at midnight by roots, worms, and dreaming children.

Her heart, too stubborn to burn, lands in a salt marsh and beats beneath the reeds, teaching the herons a red and terrible patience.

But her thoughts travel farthest. The east wind lifts them beyond maps and weather, lodging them in unopened letters, in empty chairs, in the pause before someone says her name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem in a stream-of-consciousness style about a granular woman reflecting on why she has disintegrated. Include lizard-like hours, distracted sun and stars, sparrows, and darkly comic dialogue.
counterfactuals.output:
I began as a small avalanche in a dress.

No one noticed at first. A little grit in the elevator, a pale drift beneath my chair, my left wrist shedding quietly into the soup. The waiter said, “Madam, you appear to be seasoning yourself.”

“Compliments to the chef,” I said.

That was before the lizard-like hours crawled onto the walls, green and cold-bellied, blinking one minute at a time. Noon lost its tail under the refrigerator. Three o’clock sat on a hot stone and refused to move. By evening, all the clocks were eating flies.

Why did I disintegrate?

Perhaps because I kept agreeing. Yes, I said, yes, certainly, I can make myself smaller, finer, more convenient. I can pass through the eye of your schedule. I can become a tasteful residue. I can be swept beneath the rug where the rug, at least, will know my name.

The sun was distracted that year. It rose halfway, remembered another appointment, and wandered off with its briefcase open. Papers of light blew everywhere. The stars were no better: they arrived late, glittering apologetically, whispering, “Traffic.”

“Is this death?” I asked the doctor.

He pinched a little of me between finger and thumb.

“No,” he said. “Death has better insurance.”

Outside, sparrows argued over my particles.

She was a woman, said one.

She was bread, said another.

Same thing in winter, said a third, and carried off a bright piece of my cheek.

I wanted to object, but my mouth had become a beach, every word collapsing before the water reached it. Mother, I tried to say. Marriage. Mortgage. The long hallway where I misplaced my hunger. Instead: shhhhhhh.

Maybe I came apart because I had been held together by incorrect instructions. Insert hope into slot B. Tighten until smiling. Do not expose to rain, birthdays, mirrors, or the question What do you want? If cracking persists, consult your nearest priest, mechanic, or bartender.

The bartender swept me into a little heap.

“Last call,” he said.

“I’m not drinking.”

“You’re mostly silica now. Live a little.”

So I lived a little. Then less. Then everywhere.

In the morning, the distracted sun stepped on me and swore. The lizard-like hours flicked their tongues. Sparrows rose from the pavement carrying bits of my silence in their beaks, and for one absurd second I thought: this is why—

not failure, not sorrow, not even gravity—

but distribution.

I had mistaken being one for being whole.

The broom came closer.

“Any final words?” asked the janitor.

“Yes,” I said from a thousand grains.

He leaned down.

But the stars had forgotten to turn off, the sun was rummaging through its pockets, and the sparrows were laughing too loudly.

So he swept.

And I continued.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
